question: The Saf-Ski of 1937 pioneered toe release in these devices, letting go when twisting force passed a set limit. Around 1972 a Teflon anti-friction pad began to be fitted to them, and injury rates in alpine skiing started to fall. Modern alpine versions have a toe piece, a heel piece and a brake that stops a ski running away when they release. They are set to a DIN number that depends on the skier's weight, height and ability. For 10 points, name these devices that hold a boot to a ski and, on alpine skis, release it in a fall.

This area's lifts include a trio of cable cars, 37 gondolas and 69 chairlifts, and it claims to be the largest fully connected ski area in the world. It was interconnected in 1971, and its resort La Tania was developed for the 1992 Albertville Winter Olympics. The village of Orelle, on the Maurienne side, was joined to it by a gondola between 1995 and 1997 and holds its highest point, at 3,230 metres. It lies in Savoie, in the Tarentaise, and partly within Vanoise National Park. For 10 points, name this French ski area of about 600 km of slopes that links Courchevel, Méribel, Val Thorens and Les Menuires.
answer: Les Trois Vallées [or Les 3 Vallées or Three Valleys or Trois Vallees or 3 Vallees]

question: This resort has eleven villages, and its lowest, Montchavin, sits at 1,250 metres while its highest point is the Glacier de la Chiaupe at 3,250 metres. It opened on 24 December 1961 with two drag lifts and four slopes, and a second village followed in 1969. Its bobsleigh, luge and skeleton track was built for the 1992 Albertville Winter Olympics and is due to be reused in 2030. In 2014 it was named the most popular ski resort in the world, with over 2.5 million visitors a season, and it has 225 km of slopes. For 10 points, name this French resort in Savoie which since 2003 has been linked to Les Arcs by the Vanoise Express.
answer: La Plagne [or Plagne; prompt on "Paradiski"; do not accept "Les Arcs"]

question: Its first product, the BB1, was inspired by a 1965 toy called the Snurfer and had a single strap, with a rope and handle on the nose. It was founded in 1977 in Londonderry, Vermont, where its boards were first made by hand in a garage, and it moved to Manchester, Vermont in 1978 and later to Burlington. Its founder campaigned to open lifts to snowboarders, and in 1982 Suicide Six became the first mountain to admit them. In 1985 it established the U.S. Open Snowboarding Championships, and by the 2010s it held 40 to 45 percent of the snowboard market. For 10 points, name this Vermont snowboard maker, named for the middle name of its late founder Jake Carpenter.

This mishap is a main reason why learning the sport has a reputation for being painful. It can happen on the toe side or the heel side of the board, and it is the sideways part of a rider's velocity that causes it. The steel rim on the downhill side of the board digs into the snow while the rider's body keeps moving forward, rotating them down and throwing them at the ground. Novices typically suffer it many times before they master carving turns. For 10 points, give this three-word phrase for the beginner's fall in which the downhill rim of a snowboard snags the snow.
answer: catching an edge [or catch an edge or caught an edge or catches an edge or catch edge or catching edges; prompt on "edge"]

question: It was established in 1965 by Maurice Herzog, the French mountaineer who led the 1950 expedition to Annapurna. It is a non-profit association whose members include government bodies, recreation federations and youth associations, and it is headquartered in Paris. It has a presence in about fifty countries, and about 250,000 people travel with it every year. It generally serves ages 18 to 45, though its advanced and expert courses take participants up to 55, and it also runs vocational training for outdoor careers. For 10 points, give the four-letter acronym of this French organisation that runs budget outdoor holidays, including group ski trips for young adults.
answer: UCPA [or Union nationale des centres sportifs de plein air]

question: A version of this device that detaches from its cable was introduced by a French cableway manufacturer, whose name is often used for it. Traditional ones run at up to 3.0 m/s, while detachable ones run at about 4 m/s, and they suit the low-capacity needs of beginner slopes. Unlike a rope tow, it needs no grip strength, and unlike a T-bar it uses a disc rather than a shaped bar. The disc is placed between a skier's legs so that they are pulled uphill while staying on the snow, whereas snowboarders hold it in position with their hands. For 10 points, name this device for pulling riders uphill, named for the small plastic disc that tows them up a beginner slope.
answer: button lift [or platter lift or drag lift or Poma lift or Poma; prompt on "surface lift"; do not accept "T-bar" or "rope tow"]

question: The Kohlerer Bahn in Bolzano, opened in 1908, is described as the first modern enclosed overhead transport system built solely for passengers. Its cabins are connected to a continuously circulating haul rope by spring-loaded grips, which let them slow down and detach in the stations. Monocable, bicable and tricable versions exist, and the bicable type is more stable in wind. Medellín's Metrocable and La Paz's Mi Teleférico use this kind of system as public transport. For 10 points, name this kind of ski-resort transport system with enclosed cabins, unlike a chairlift, which shares its name with a boat of Venice.
answer: gondola [or gondola lift or gondolas; prompt on "aerial lift" or "cable car"; do not accept "chairlift"]

question: Although the English name of the sport comes from Old Norse by way of Norwegian, this custom has a French name. The name was chosen because of the early popularity of such activities in the French Alps. It is most popular in Alpine regions, though it has spread to mountain destinations all over the world. Visitors often stop at bars on their last descent of the day while still wearing all of their slope gear. For 10 points, give this French term for the drinking, dancing and other socializing at a mountain resort once the lifts have closed.
answer: après-ski [or apres ski or apres-ski or après ski or apres; prompt on "nightlife"]

question: These were adapted from workwear that emerged in the 1890s through Levi Strauss & Co. and became common among farmers, miners, loggers and railroad workers during the Great Depression. That original garment was usually made of denim, though corduroy, chino cloth or leather were also used. The adapted versions are made of wind- and waterproof fabric and have adjustable shoulder braces. The British name for the original garment differs from this French-derived term. For 10 points, give this French-derived term for shoulder-braced overtrousers worn for skiing, sailing and diving.
answer: salopettes [or salopette; prompt on "ski pants" or "bib pants" or "dungarees" or "overalls"]

question: This substance is applied to the underside of winter-sports equipment to adjust its coefficient of friction for the day's snow conditions. Classic cross-country competitors use a grip-enhancing variant during their forward stride, choosing a hard formulation for fresh snow and sticky klister for old or wet snow. Its other main form, used by both alpine and cross-country athletes, instead minimizes sliding friction and has historically been made from paraffin, later joined by fluorocarbons and graphite. Applying it also fills in scratches and gouges that rocks and ice leave in the equipment's base. For 10 points, name this substance athletes melt or rub onto their equipment's underside.

Founded in 1947 in Annecy in a one-room metalworking shop, this company began by making steel ski edges before founder François's son Georges took the reins. Its 1957 Skade toe piece transformed ski bindings, helping it become the world's leading binding manufacturer by 1972. It later branched into footwear with the 1979 SX90 boot and into cross-country gear with the 1980 SNS system. Adidas bought the company in 1997 before selling it to Amer Sports in 2005. For 10 points, name this French sporting-goods company, a major maker of ski bindings, boots and boards.

Created in 1974, this winter-sport consortium spans roughly 3,000 square kilometres of northeastern Italy and unites twelve separate resorts under one lift pass. Around 97 percent of its 1,246 kilometres of slopes are covered by snowmaking, guaranteeing downhill access from December to April even without fresh snowfall. Its 450 lifts make it, by total piste length, the largest linked downhill area in the world, spanning limestone peaks in northeastern Italy. For 10 points, give the name of this Italian multi-resort lift pass.

A former ski instructor named Luc Reversade founded this on-mountain establishment in Val d'Isère in 1974 with his mother and a chef named Mamone, after visiting party spots in Ibiza, Turkey and Miami for inspiration. Its 1980 addition of an open-air bar, paired with live music and elaborately costumed dancers performing on tabletops, turned it into a full-blown daytime clubbing experience. Its original Val d'Isère outpost sits at 2,400 metres, and the concept has since expanded to Val Thorens, Méribel, Les Arcs and Alpe d'Huez. For 10 points, name this chain of raucous French mountainside restaurant-bars whose name translates to "the sweet madness."

This city's airport, established in 1919 and given a terminal building in 1946, has an unusual bi-national layout that lets arriving passengers walk directly into either of two countries. It handled nearly 17.8 million passengers in 2024 and serves as the busiest air gateway to the Portes du Soleil, the Mont Blanc massif and the Tarentaise Valley's ski resorts. Straddling the Swiss-French border, it is the closest major airport to Chamonix, Verbier and Morzine. For 10 points, name this Swiss city on its namesake lake, headquarters to numerous international organizations.

Standing at an official height of 4,807 metres, this peak on the French-Italian border was first summited on 8 August 1786 by Michel-Gabriel Paccard and Jacques Balmat, an ascent often called the birth of mountaineering. It towers just south of the resort town of Chamonix and is nicknamed the Roof of Europe. For 10 points, name this highest peak in the Alps and in Western Europe, whose French name literally means "white mountain."

This portmanteau term describes snow produced when cold air masses from Siberia cross the Sea of Japan, pick up moisture, and are forced upward by Japan's mountain ranges, cooling rapidly into exceptionally light, dry flakes. Riders sometimes call the month of peak conditions for it "Japanuary." It is especially prized in Hokkaido, where resorts advertise its high volume and fine, dry texture as superior to typical Alpine or North American snow. For 10 points, give this slang blend of a country's name with a word for fresh, fluffy snow.

This ski area occupies a single mountain in Hokkaido and comprises four separately managed resorts. Hokkaido's first unified lift-ticket system, the Free Passport, launched here in November 1993, and by 1998 it had grown into an All Mountain Pass covering every lift across all four areas. Tokyu Land Corporation has controlled Grand Hirafu since 2004, while a Hong Kong real-estate firm has run Hanazono since 2007, yet skiers can move seamlessly across shared terrain linking every resort. For 10 points, name this Hokkaido ski area, famed among powder-hunters for its Japow, whose four resorts share a name with the surrounding town.

This area's Happo-One resort hosted the men's downhill, super-G and combined alpine skiing events, along with ski jumping, at the 1998 Winter Olympics. Today it comprises ten interconnected resorts served by 92 lifts and 137 runs stretched across some 30 kilometres, and it receives over 11 metres of snowfall a year. It lies in the same prefecture that hosted those 1998 Games. For 10 points, name this Japanese winter-sports area, home to the Happo-One resort.

Australians Matthew Hampton and Mick Klima founded this ski and snowboard rental and retail company in 2005, eventually opening seven stores across Niseko, Hakuba and Furano. In 2022 it was acquired in full by the American outdoor retailer Evo, after which Hampton joined Evo's leadership team as managing director for the Asia-Pacific region. It equips travelers who arrive without their own gear to chase the region's famous powder snow. For 10 points, name this ski and snowboard rental chain, whose name is also a word for a regular, repeated pattern in music.

The system that uses this rating grew out of research the Walt Disney Company conducted for a ski resort it planned to build in California's Mineral King Valley, which was never constructed. Testing skiers' reactions to shapes and colors, that research concluded a circle read as soft and a square as more rigid, while this shape read as the most serious. Adopted by the National Ski Areas Association in 1968, it marks the steepest, narrowest and often mogul-covered terrain on a trail map, reserved for expert-only runs. A single version of this symbol denotes merely 'advanced' terrain; using two signals the most difficult trails a resort offers. For 10 points, name this trail rating, marked by two of a shape more commonly seen on playing cards, denoting a resort's most difficult terrain.

Because a snowboarder's feet are locked into fixed bindings, this term and another one borrowed from skateboarding are used almost interchangeably in that sport, even though skateboarders and some skiers draw a sharper line between the two. A snowboarder with a regular stance, who normally leads with the left foot, performs it by leading with the right foot instead, and a snowboarder with a goofy stance does the reverse. Approaching a jump or a rail in this stance is considered a mark of a well-rounded athlete, since it requires relearning balance with the trailing foot forward. For 10 points, give this term, meaning to descend on a snowboard or skis in the stance opposite your natural one.

This trick is popped from the nose of the board rather than the tail, and can be attempted on jumps as small as the knuckle of a landing or even a simple roller. It is essentially a straight frontflip, or sometimes a sideflip, and its name is meant as the more docile-sounding counterpart to a similar trick called the 'wildcat,' a straight backflip popped from the tail. Despite the implication of its name, riders are warned it is not for the faint of heart. For 10 points, give this snowboarding trick named for a domesticated canine, the front-flipping counterpart to the 'wildcat.'

This stance's name is traced to a 1950s Disney short in which the cartoon character for whom it's named is shown surfing with his right side leading. It describes a boardsport rider who leads on the right and pushes or trails on the left, the opposite of the far more common 'regular' stance. The distinction applies across skateboarding, snowboarding and surfing, and riding this way is not considered incorrect, only less common, since which way feels natural varies rider to rider. For 10 points, give this Disney-derived term for a right-side-leading board stance, the opposite of 'regular.'

Slopes of this type are not groomed, marked, checked for avalanche danger, or patrolled, unlike the runs they're contrasted with. Many of the best stashes of untouched snow found this way sit on slopes between roughly 30 and 45 degrees, the same steepness most prone to avalanches, so guides recommend hiring someone who knows the area's snowpack before venturing there. This term describes descending on terrain outside a resort's maintained trail network, whether inside or beyond the resort's boundary. For 10 points, give this French-derived term for descending away from marked, patrolled runs.

The word at the center of this phrase, meaning a blend of style and ease, dates back to at least 1995, when Method Man used it in a verse, and it was later sampled in a 1998 Gang Starr track. Skiers and snowboarders borrowed the word to describe looking effortlessly cool while riding, and this particular saying became a tongue-in-cheek defense of bare-headed riders, though it's disputed by those who insist safety gear can be stylish too. Plastered across ski-and-snowboard-culture memes and videos, it pairs a piece of safety equipment with that slang word for style. For 10 points, give this ironic four-word ski and snowboard culture catchphrase claiming that going bare-headed looks cooler.

Merriam-Webster traces the first recorded use of this phrase to 1860, defining it simply as clear, cloudless weather, though skiers have since narrowed its meaning. Because the songbird in its name is native to North America, the phrase is believed to have originated there before spreading to ski culture worldwide. Skiers and snowboarders use it specifically for the clear, calm, sunny conditions that often follow a snowstorm, when fresh powder blankets the slopes. For 10 points, give this two-word term, named for a songbird, describing ideal sunny powder conditions on the slopes.

These maintenance paths owe their name to a 1940s Tucker snow-vehicle trademark, which became a generic term for the crawler machines that prepare resort terrain overnight. Typically narrow, flatter and gentler than the runs around them, they connect separate trails or ferry skiers across a mountain that a lift doesn't directly reach. The same vehicles that inspired their name are sometimes also used to carry skiers deep into the backcountry for a fee. For 10 points, give this term for a narrow, groomed connector path at a ski resort, named for the snow vehicle that carves it.

A blade dragging against the snow as this kind of slope is prepared leaves behind the ridged pattern nicknamed 'corduroy,' beloved by early-morning skiers for the smooth, even surface it provides. Unprepared, ungraded descents are typically contrasted with these more heavily managed slopes, which have been mechanically broken up and packed down overnight by a tracked vehicle towing a tiller. The same word can also refer to that packing vehicle itself, though skiers more often use it for the surface that vehicle leaves behind. For 10 points, give this term for a slope whose snow has been mechanically packed and smoothed, as opposed to steep, bumpy or powder terrain.

The word for these terrain features comes from a Bavarian and Austrian German word for a small mound or hillock, and while they can be built artificially, they usually form naturally as riders carve sharp turns and push snow into repeated mounds. A freestyle discipline built entirely around navigating them, launching off them for jumps, and descending them for speed and rhythm became an FIS-recognized sport in 1979 and a medal event at the 1992 Albertville Olympics. For 10 points, give this term for the repeated bumps that form on a steep descent, and the Olympic freestyle event contested on them.

Overhanging branches prevent snow from piling evenly around a trunk, creating this hazard: a pocket of loose, unconsolidated snow that can swallow a skier or rider who falls in headfirst. Deaths from falling into one are classified separately from avalanche fatalities, under the acronym NARSID, for non-avalanche-related snow immersion death, and are most common in the deep snowpacks of western North America. Victims can suffocate within fifteen to thirty minutes, often from a buildup of carbon dioxide rather than a lack of oxygen, which is why experts urge riding with a partner who keeps you in sight at all times. For 10 points, name this snow-covered hazard found at the base of trunks in deep powder.

Founded in 1968 in Bern, Switzerland, this organization began as an alliance of ten national purchasing centers from countries including Belgium, Germany, France and Sweden, pooling their buying power for sporting goods. In 1984 it launched McKinley, one of its largest private-label brands, as part of a push beyond collective purchasing into house-brand product development. Today it operates through more than five thousand specialist stores across some forty countries, making it one of the largest sporting goods retailers in the world. For 10 points, name this Swiss-headquartered retail group and ski-and-snowboard-gear chain whose name literally suggests sport between nations.

According to local legend, this area's name came from a stockman's complaint after he was caught in a deadly blizzard on these slopes in the nineteenth century. A Norwegian settler built the area's first rope tow in 1952, and a permanent T-bar followed in 1958, developments spurred by the Snowy Mountains Hydro-Electric Scheme that opened up the region. In March 1995 it merged with the neighboring areas of Smiggin Holes, Mount Blue Cow and Guthega, along with the Skitube alpine railway, to form a single operation. For 10 points, name this Australian winter-sports destination, the largest of its kind in the Southern Hemisphere.
